```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(modelcompR)
```

This article covers everything that happens before `mtkcompile()`: declaring
the independent variable, unknowns, parameters and constants with their
metadata; writing equations; assembling them into a `System`; querying a
system; building hierarchical models from components; connecting components
through connectors; checking units; and working with the expressions
through symcompR. Each part names the ModelingToolkit (MTK) construct it
corresponds to. The article ends with an RC circuit assembled from
components and simulated.

Accessors such as `equations()` and `unknowns()` return plain R lists. To
print them one per line, this article uses a small helper:

```{r}
pp <- function(x) writeLines(vapply(x, format, ""))
```

## The independent variable and the derivative

In MTK, `using ModelingToolkit: t_nounits as t, D_nounits as D` gives the
time variable and its derivative operator. modelcompR exports the same two
objects. The name `t` is not exported because it would mask `base::t()`;
assign the objects to short names in your own code instead.

```{r}
t <- t_nounits
D <- D_nounits
t
D
getdescription(t)
```

`Differential(iv)` builds the derivative operator for any independent
variable, and `independent_variable()` declares new ones, the
`@independent_variables` macro. Powers of the operator give higher
derivatives. Derivatives of unknowns stay unevaluated; `expand_derivatives()`
applies the chain rule to expressions around them.

```{r}
s <- independent_variable("s")
Ds <- Differential(s)
Ds
variables("pos(t)")
D(D(pos))
Differential(t, 2)(pos)
expand_derivatives(D(pos^2 + sin(t)))
```

## Declaring variables and parameters from strings

`variables()` and `parameters()` are the R counterparts of `@variables` and
`@parameters`. Each argument is a declaration string; the function creates
the symbol and assigns it in the calling environment, so `x` below is an
ordinary R object afterwards. A name followed by `(t)` depends on the
independent variable `t`, which is looked up in the calling environment.

```{r}
variables("x(t) = 1", "y(t)")
parameters("k = 0.5", "m")
x
k
getdefault(x)
hasdefault(y)
```

The text after `=` is evaluated as R code in the calling environment, so a
default can be a number, a symbolic expression of other variables, or `NA`.
These three cases mean different things. A numeric default becomes an
initial condition (or a parameter value) of every system the variable
appears in. A symbolic default becomes a binding: the variable is then
determined by that expression. `NA` is Julia's `missing`: the value is
unknown and is solved for during initialization.

```{r}
parameters("k2 = 2 * k", "kfree = NA")
getdefault(k2)
getdefault(kfree)
```

Array variables are written with a range after the declaration. They are
returned as a list of scalar variables `z[1]`, `z[2]`, and so on, and a
vector default is split over the elements.

```{r}
variables("z(t)[1:3] = c(1, 2, 3)")
z
getdefault(z[[3]])
```

The `.meta` argument attaches the same metadata to every variable in the
call. For metadata that differs per variable, use `Variable()` (next
section).

```{r}
variables("ua(t)", "ub(t)", .meta = list(description = "a state", bounds = c(0, 1)))
getdescription(ua)
getbounds(ub)
```

`constants()` declares constants (`@constants`), `brownians()` declares
Brownian variables for stochastic models (`@brownians`), and `discretes()`
declares discrete parameters (`@discretes`): parameters that events are
allowed to change.

```{r}
constants("c0 = 299792458")
brownians("wn")
isconstant(c0)
isbrownian(wn)
```

## Variable(), Parameter() and metadata

`Variable()` and `Parameter()` declare one symbol and return it, without
assigning anything; `Variable("x", t, default = 1)` is `@variables x(t) = 1`.
Every metadata field of MTK has an argument.

```{r}
pos2 <- Variable("pos2", t,
  default = 1, guess = 0.5, bounds = c(0, 10),
  description = "position of the cart", state_priority = 5,
  irreducible = TRUE, input = FALSE)
getdefault(pos2)
getguess(pos2)
getbounds(pos2)
getdescription(pos2)
state_priority(pos2)
isirreducible(pos2)
isinput(pos2)
isoutput(pos2)
```

The meaning of the fields:

* `default`: initial condition or binding, as described above.
* `guess`: starting value for the nonlinear solve of initialization, for
  variables that are solved for rather than given.
* `bounds`: `c(lower, upper)`, used by optimization and some solvers.
* `description` and `unit`: documentation, and the input of unit checking
  (see the units section).
* `input`, `output`, `disturbance`: causal roles, used by causal
  connections, linearization and control function generation.
* `irreducible`: the variable is kept as an unknown by `mtkcompile()` even
  when it could be eliminated.
* `state_priority`: a number; higher values are preferred as
  differential states during index reduction.
* `connect`: `Flow` or `Stream` for connector variables (see connectors).
* `tunable` (parameters only): whether the parameter is exposed as tunable,
  `TRUE` by default. Further fields such as `dist`, `nominal` and `misc`
  pass through `...`.

```{r}
damp <- Parameter("damp", default = 0.1, tunable = FALSE, dist = "Uniform(0, 1)")
istunable(damp)
getdist(damp)
getnominal(damp)
isparameter(damp)
isvariable(pos2)
```

`Constant()` declares a constant (`@constants`): a parameter kind that
always has a value and is never tunable. `Brownian()`, `Poissonian()` and
`Discrete()` are the single symbol forms of the other kinds.

```{r}
grav0 <- Constant("grav0", 9.81, description = "standard gravity")
isconstant(grav0)
Discrete("count", t, default = 0)
```

Metadata can be read and changed after declaration. `getmetadata()` and
`setmetadata()` are the general forms; the `set*` functions return a copy
of the variable and also update the package registry, so the new value is
seen wherever the name appears. The names of the metadata keys are
exported as `VariableUnit`, `VariableBounds` and so on, for code ported from
MTK.

```{r}
pos2 <- setguess(pos2, 0.25)
getguess(pos2)
pos2 <- setmetadata(pos2, "misc", list(color = "red"))
getmetadata(pos2, "misc")
VariableBounds
```

`toparam()` turns a variable into a parameter with the same name and
metadata, and `tovar()` does the reverse.

```{r}
isparameter(toparam(pos2))
isvariable(tovar(damp))
```

Metadata is attached to the returned object and also stored in a registry
keyed by the variable name, which is how a bare symbol found inside an
expression recovers its metadata. Declaring the same name twice with
different metadata replaces the registry entry, so give distinct quantities
distinct names.

## Operators on variables: Initial and Pre

`Initial(x)` stands for the initial value of `x`. A compiled system gets a
parameter `Initial(x)` for each such reference, and these parameters are
hidden from `parameters()` unless `initial_parameters = TRUE` is passed.
`Pre(x)` is the value just before an event, used in event affects (see the
events article).

```{r}
Initial(x)
isinitial(Initial(x))
Pre(x)
```

A typical use binds a parameter to the initial value of an algebraic
variable. Here `zi` is determined by `zi^3 + zi = xi`, and the rate `r` is
fixed to whatever `zi` is at the start.

```{r}
xi <- Variable("xi", t); zi <- Variable("zi", t); r <- Parameter("r")
ib <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(xi) ~ -r * xi, 0 ~ zi^3 + zi - xi), t,
                        name = "ib", bindings = list(r ~ Initial(zi)),
                        guesses = list(zi ~ 1)))
pp(parameters(ib))
pp(parameters(ib, initial_parameters = TRUE))
prob <- ODEProblem(ib, list(xi ~ 2), c(0, 1))
c(prob[zi], prob$ps[r])
```

The value `zi = 1` solves `zi^3 + zi = 2`, so `r` is 1.

## Equations

An equation is written as an R formula, exactly as in Julia: `D(x) ~ -k * x`.
Both sides are evaluated in the environment where the formula was created.
`Equation(lhs, rhs)` builds the same object explicitly, and `as_equation()`
converts a formula.

```{r}
e1 <- Equation(D(x), -k * x)
e1
class(e1)
e2 <- as_equation(D(y) ~ x - y)
eq_lhs(e2)
eq_rhs(e2)
```

An equation whose sides are arrays is expanded elementwise, and a scalar
side is broadcast.

```{r}
print(as_equation(D(z) ~ -z))
```

Equations that contain a derivative of an unknown are differential
equations; the others are algebraic.

```{r}
is_diff_equation(e2)
is_alg_equation(as_equation(0 ~ x^2 + y^2 - 1))
```

`Inequality()`, with the shorthands `%<~%` and `%>~%` (Julia's `≲` and
`≳`), states constraints for optimization problems.

```{r}
(x^2 + y^2) %<~% 1
```

## Systems

`System(eqs, iv, ...)` is the single system type of MTK 11. With an
independent variable it describes differential, differential algebraic,
stochastic, jump, delay or discrete equations; without one it is a
nonlinear system, or an optimization problem when `costs` are given. A name
is required; it plays the role of `@named`.

```{r}
variables("q(t) = 1", "qv(t)", "qe(t)")
parameters("kq = 2", "cq")
osc <- System(
  list(D(q) ~ qv, D(qv) ~ -kq * q - cq * qv, qe ~ kq * q^2 / 2 + qv^2 / 2), t,
  name = "osc",
  initial_conditions = list(qv ~ 0.5),
  bindings = list(cq ~ kq / 10),
  guesses = list(qv ~ 0))
osc
```

When `unknowns` and `ps` are not given they are inferred from the
equations: declared parameters become parameters and everything that
depends on `t` becomes an unknown. The variable maps take formulas
`x ~ value`, pairs `list(x, value)` or named lists. Defaults declared on
the variables are collected automatically: `q` brings its default 1, and
`kq` its default 2.

The accessors have the MTK names.

```{r}
pp(unknowns(osc))
pp(parameters(osc))
pp(equations(osc))
get_iv(osc)
independent_variables(osc)
nameof(osc)
```

`initial_conditions()`, `bindings()` and `guesses()` return variable maps.
`defaults()` merges the first two, as the older MTK API did, and
`bound_parameters()` lists the parameters that have a binding.

```{r}
initial_conditions(osc)
bindings(osc)
guesses(osc)
defaults(osc)
pp(bound_parameters(osc))
```

`set_defaults()` returns a copy with extra initial conditions.

```{r}
initial_conditions(set_defaults(osc, q ~ 3))
```

`names()` lists what `$` can reach: subsystems, unknowns, parameters and
observed variables.

```{r}
names(osc)
```

### Compiled systems, observed and full equations

`mtkcompile()` simplifies a system structurally. Equations that only define
a variable, such as the energy `qe` above, are removed from the equations
and kept as observed equations, and `qe` is no longer an unknown.

```{r}
osc_c <- mtkcompile(osc)
osc_c
pp(observed(osc_c))
pp(observables(osc_c))
iscomplete(osc)
iscomplete(osc_c)
```

`full_equations()` substitutes the observed equations into the equations.
The difference shows when an observed variable appears on a right hand
side. Observed equations can also be given to `System()` directly through
`observed`:

```{r}
variables("w1(t) = 1", "w2(t)")
fe <- System(list(D(w1) ~ -w2), t, observed = list(w2 ~ 2 * w1), name = "fe")
pp(equations(fe))
pp(full_equations(fe))
```

The RC circuit at the end shows the same on a compiled model. A compiled
system is turned into a problem directly, and observed variables can be
read from the solution:

```{r}
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(osc_c, list(), c(0, 2)))
sol$retcode
sol(2)
sol(2, idxs = qe)
```

### Own fields and hierarchical accessors

`equations()`, `unknowns()`, `parameters()`, `observed()` and the variable
map accessors include all subsystems, namespaced. The `get_*` functions,
such as `get_eqs()` and `get_unknowns()`, and the `*_toplevel` functions
return only the system's own entries. `diff_equations()` and
`alg_equations()` split the equations by kind.

```{r}
pp(diff_equations(osc))
pp(alg_equations(osc))
length(get_systems(osc))
```

## Hierarchical models

### Components are R functions

MTK's `@component` functions and `@mtkmodel` blocks become ordinary R
functions that take a `name` and return a `System`. The variables are
declared inside the function, so every instance gets its own copy.

```{r}
Decay <- function(name, rate = 1) {
  x <- Variable("x", t, default = 1)
  kd <- Parameter("kd", default = rate)
  System(list(D(x) ~ -kd * x), t, name = name)
}
a <- Decay("a", rate = 1)
b <- Decay("b", rate = 2)
```

`compose(sys, ...)` adds subsystems to a system; passing `systems =` to
`System()` does the same. The variables of a subsystem are namespaced with
its name and the separator `₊`, as in MTK.

```{r}
top <- compose(System(list(), t, name = "top"), a, b)
top
hierarchy(top)
pp(equations(top))
```

### Namespaced access with `$`

`sys$sub$x` is Julia's `sys.sub.x`. On a system that is not complete, the
result is namespaced from the top, which is the form needed when writing
equations in an enclosing system. `nonamespace()` returns the variable as
written inside the subsystem (`@nonamespace`), and `renamespace()` adds a
prefix explicitly.

```{r}
top$a$x
nonamespace(top$a$x)
renamespace("plant", a$x)
```

Once a system is complete (after `complete()` or `mtkcompile()`), `$` no
longer adds the top level name, since the problem is built from that
system; `namespace()` forces the full name when needed. `flatten()`
collapses the hierarchy into one system with namespaced variables.

```{r}
top_c <- complete(top)
top_c$a$x
namespace(top_c$a$x)
flatten(top)
```

Inside a component it is often convenient to read the variables of a
subsystem without its prefix. `toggle_namespacing(sys, FALSE)` returns a
copy whose `$` access does not namespace; the RC circuit below uses this to
extend a base component.

### named()

`named(sys <- Constructor(...))` calls the constructor with
`name = "sys"` and assigns the result, the `@named` macro. Symbolic
arguments are wrapped in `ParentScope()`, so a parameter passed into a
component refers to the parameter of the enclosing system.

```{r}
Lag1 <- function(name, gain) {
  xl <- Variable("xl", t, default = 0)
  System(list(D(xl) ~ gain - xl), t, name = name)
}
kshared <- Parameter("kshared", default = 3)
named(lag1 <- Lag1(gain = kshared))
nameof(lag1)
pp(parameters(System(list(), t, systems = list(lag1), name = "plant")))
```

The parameter appears as `kshared`, not `lag1₊kshared`.

### extend()

`extend(sys, base)` merges the equations, variables, maps and subsystems of
`base` into `sys`; it is Julia's `extend`, used by `@extend`. Inheritance
of a common interface (the `OnePort` of the circuit library below) is
written this way.

```{r}
Base1 <- function(name) {
  xb <- Variable("xb", t, default = 0)
  System(list(), t, list(xb), list(), name = name)
}
base1 <- Base1("base1")
u <- toggle_namespacing(base1, FALSE)
ext <- extend(System(list(D(u$xb) ~ 1), t, name = "ext"), base1)
ext
```

### component() and mtkmodel()

`component(f)` marks a constructor as a component; the systems it builds
record the constructor name in their metadata, as `@component` does.
`rename_system()` changes the name of an existing system.

```{r}
DecayC <- component(Decay)
get_metadata(DecayC(name = "dc"))$gui_metadata
nameof(rename_system(a, "a2"))
```

`mtkmodel()` builds a constructor from declarations, the counterpart of an
`@mtkmodel` block. Declarations are strings as in `variables()`, blocks such
as `equations` are quoted expressions evaluated where the declarations are
bound, and the constructor's arguments override the declared defaults.

```{r}
Lag <- mtkmodel("Lag",
  parameters = list("tau = 1"),
  variables = list("xm(t) = 0", "um(t)"),
  equations = quote(list(D(xm) ~ (um - xm) / tau, um ~ 1)))
Lag
lag <- Lag(name = "lag", tau = 0.5)
initial_conditions(lag)
```

## Scopes

By default, a variable used in a subsystem belongs to that subsystem and is
namespaced with it (`LocalScope`). `ParentScope(x)` makes it refer to the
variable of the same name one level up, and `GlobalScope(x)` to the top
level variable. Nested `ParentScope()` calls go up further levels.

```{r}
Sub <- function(name) {
  xs <- Variable("xs", t)
  pg <- GlobalScope(Parameter("pg"))
  pp_ <- ParentScope(Parameter("pp_"))
  pl <- Parameter("pl")
  System(list(D(xs) ~ -pg * pp_ * pl * xs), t, name = name)
}
mid <- System(list(), t, systems = list(Sub("sub")), name = "mid")
outer <- System(list(), t, systems = list(mid), name = "outer")
pp(equations(outer))
pp(parameters(outer))
```

`pl` is local to `sub`, `pp_` belongs to `mid`, and `pg` to the top.
`collect_scoped_vars()` lists the variables of a system that refer to the
enclosing system. A scope can also be applied to a symbolic default:
`2 * ParentScope(kg)` passed as a parameter value binds the component's
parameter to the parent's `kg`.

```{r}
kg <- Parameter("kg", default = 3)
d1 <- Decay("d1", rate = 2 * ParentScope(kg))
bindings(System(list(), t, systems = list(d1), name = "host"))
```

## Connectors and connections

Acausal models connect components through connectors: small systems whose
variables are shared at a connection. `connector(f)` marks a constructor as
a connector (`@connector`). In `connect(a, b, ...)`, potential variables
(connect type `"Equality"`, the default) are set equal, and variables with
`connect = Flow` sum to zero, entering with a negative sign when the
connector is on the outside of the system that holds the connection.
`connector_type()` classifies a connector.

```{r}
Pin <- connector(function(name) {
  v <- Variable("v", t)
  i <- Variable("i", t, connect = Flow)
  System(list(), t, list(v, i), list(), name = name)
})
pa <- Pin(name = "pa")
connector_type(pa)
getconnect(nonamespace(pa$i))
connect(pa, Pin(name = "pb"))
```

A connection is placed directly in the equation list.
`expand_connections()` replaces it by equations; `mtkcompile()` does this
automatically. Here two components each have one pin and inject a fixed
current:

```{r}
Terminal <- function(name, i0) {
  p <- Pin(name = "p")
  System(list(p$i ~ i0), t, systems = list(p), name = name)
}
ta <- Terminal("ta", 1)
tb <- Terminal("tb", -1)
joint <- System(list(connect(ta$p, tb$p)), t, systems = list(ta, tb), name = "joint")
pp(equations(expand_connections(joint)))
```

The voltages are set equal and the currents into the joint sum to zero. A
connector that is a direct subsystem of the system holding the connection,
the outside connector of a composite component, enters the current balance
with a negative sign, and a connector left unconnected gets zero flow.

### Causal connections

`connect()` also joins causal variables marked `output` and `input`; the
first argument is the output and the others are inputs, each of which is
set equal to it.

```{r}
yo <- Variable("yo", t, output = TRUE)
ui <- Variable("ui", t, input = TRUE)
src <- System(list(yo ~ sin(t)), t, name = "src")
xk <- Variable("xk", t)
filt <- System(list(D(xk) ~ ui - xk), t, name = "filt")
loop <- System(list(connect(src$yo, filt$ui)), t, systems = list(src, filt), name = "loop")
pp(equations(expand_connections(loop)))
```

### Stream variables

Variables with `connect = Stream` carry a quantity transported by a flow,
such as specific enthalpy in a fluid port. A connector with stream
variables may have at most one flow variable. `instream(h)` is the value of
`h` flowing into the connector, which `expand_connections()` resolves with
the mixing rule of the Modelica specification.

```{r}
Port <- connector(function(name) {
  P <- Variable("P", t)
  mf <- Variable("mf", t, connect = Flow)
  hs <- Variable("hs", t, connect = Stream)
  System(list(), t, list(P, mf, hs), list(), name = name)
})
connector_type(Port(name = "tmp"))
Reservoir <- function(name, h0, m0) {
  port <- Port(name = "port")
  hin <- Variable("hin", t)
  System(list(port$hs ~ h0, hin ~ instream(port$hs), port$mf ~ m0, port$P ~ 1), t,
         list(hin), list(), systems = list(port), name = name)
}
r1 <- Reservoir("r1", h0 = 2, m0 = -1)
r2 <- Reservoir("r2", h0 = 3, m0 = 1)
pipe <- System(list(connect(r1$port, r2$port)), t, systems = list(r1, r2), name = "pipe")
pp(equations(expand_connections(pipe)))
```

With two connectors the rule is simple: what flows into one is what the
other emits, so `r1₊hin` is `r2₊port₊hs`. With three or more, `instream`
becomes a flow weighted average.

`domain_connect()` connects domains only (a fluid with shared properties,
say): it shares the parameters of a domain source connector without
generating equations.

## Units

Units are strings in the `unit` metadata: SI base and derived units with SI
prefixes, products, quotients and powers, such as `"m/s^2"`, `"kJ"` or
`"ms"`. `get_unit()` propagates units through an expression and signals a
`ValidationError` when they are inconsistent. As in MTK with
DynamicQuantities, units must agree exactly: `"kJ"` and `"J"` are
different. To use units on derivatives, the independent variable needs a
unit too; here a separate time variable `ts` is declared so that `t` keeps
no unit.

```{r}
ts <- setmetadata(independent_variable("ts"), "unit", "s")
Dts <- Differential(ts)
hgt <- Variable("hgt", ts, unit = "m")
vel <- Variable("vel", ts, unit = "m/s")
grav <- Parameter("grav", unit = "m/s^2", default = 9.81)
get_unit(vel / ts)
get_unit(grav * ts^2)
get_unit(Dts(hgt))
```

`validate()` checks an expression, equation, list of equations or system.
It returns `TRUE`, or warns about each inconsistent equation and returns
`FALSE`.

```{r}
validate(list(Dts(hgt) ~ vel, Dts(vel) ~ -grav))
validate(Dts(hgt) ~ grav)
```

Functions such as `exp` need dimensionless arguments, and the terms of a
sum must have the same unit.

```{r}
tryCatch(get_unit(hgt + vel), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
class(tryCatch(get_unit(exp(hgt)), error = function(e) e))[1]
```

`System()` runs the unit check whenever a variable carries a unit, and
stops on an inconsistency. The `checks` argument takes the flags
`CheckAll`, `CheckNone`, `CheckComponents` and `CheckUnits`, combined with
`bitwOr()`; `CheckComponents` alone keeps the structural checks and skips
the units.

```{r}
fall <- System(list(Dts(hgt) ~ vel, Dts(vel) ~ -grav), ts, name = "fall")
validate(fall)
try(System(list(Dts(hgt) ~ grav), ts, name = "bad"))
System(list(Dts(hgt) ~ grav), ts, name = "unchecked", checks = CheckComponents)
```

## Working with symcompR

Expressions in modelcompR are symcompR expressions (class `sym`): `x(t)` is
the application of an undefined function to `t`, and a parameter is a
symbol. The symcompR functions that take expressions therefore work on
them.

```{r}
class(x)
simplify((x^2 - 1) / (x - 1))
simplify(sin(x)^2 + cos(x)^2)
expand((x + k)^2)
factor_sym(x^2 - k^2)
diff(k * x^2, x)
diff(k * x^2, k)
subs(k * x^2, k, 3)
```

`latex()` takes an expression; apply it to each side of an equation.

```{r}
eq <- as_equation(D(x) ~ -k * x^2 / m)
paste(latex(eq_lhs(eq)), "=", latex(eq_rhs(eq)))
```

modelcompR adds a few helpers of its own, named after Symbolics.jl:
`get_variables()` lists the variables of an expression, `collect_vars()`
splits them into unknowns and parameters, `substitute_vars()` substitutes
(MTK's `substitute`, renamed to keep `base::substitute`), `toexpr()`
converts to R code, `Term()` builds a call of a symbolic function, and
`build_function()` compiles an expression to an R function of a numeric
vector. Use `build_function()` rather than symcompR's `lambdify()` for
expressions that contain `x(t)`.

```{r}
pp(get_variables(D(x) ~ -k * x + t))
str(lapply(collect_vars(D(x) ~ -k * sin(x), t), function(v) vapply(v, format, "")))
substitute_vars(-k * x, list(k ~ 2))
toexpr(D(x) ~ -k * sin(x))
Term("f", k, 2)
f <- build_function(-k * x^2, list(x, k))
f(c(2, 3))
```

Symbols and functions created with symcompR directly can be used in
models. An undefined function applied to `t` is an unknown, as in MTK. A
bare symbol is an unknown of a system without an independent variable;
in a time dependent system it is rejected, since it is not a function of
`t` and is not declared as a parameter.

```{r}
fx <- symcompR::Function("fx")(t)
System(list(D(fx) ~ -k * fx), t, name = "from_symcompr")
sy <- symcompR::Symbol("sy")
System(list(0 ~ sy^2 - k), name = "nonlinear")
```

### Masking rules

No modelcompR export masks a function of base R or of the packages R
attaches by default; that is why time is `t_nounits` and MTK's `substitute`
is `substitute_vars()`. A few names are shared with symcompR, and
`library(modelcompR)` reports the functions among them as masked:

```{r}
intersect(getNamespaceExports("modelcompR"), getNamespaceExports("symcompR"))
```

`Stream` is a string value in modelcompR (the connect type), so a call
`Stream(...)` still reaches symcompR's function. Each of the other names is
a function that hands arguments that are not modelcompR objects to the
symcompR function, so both packages can be attached together: `compose()`
of two expressions is symcompR's function composition, and `flatten()` of a
list flattens the list.

```{r}
compose(sy^2, sy + 1)
unlist(flatten(list(1, list(2, 3))))
```

## Worked example: an RC circuit from components

This is the acausal component tutorial of MTK. A `Pin` carries a voltage
and a current (a flow variable). `OnePort` is the common interface of two
terminal elements: the voltage across it and the current through it.
`Resistor`, `Capacitor` and `ConstantVoltage` extend `OnePort` with their
constitutive equation, and `Ground` fixes the voltage of one pin to zero.

```{r}
Pin <- connector(function(name) {
  v <- Variable("v", t)
  i <- Variable("i", t, connect = Flow)
  System(list(), t, list(v, i), list(), name = name)
})

Ground <- component(function(name) {
  g <- Pin(name = "g")
  System(list(g$v ~ 0), t, list(), list(), systems = list(g), name = name)
}, type = "Ground")

OnePort <- function(name) {
  p <- Pin(name = "p")
  n <- Pin(name = "n")
  v <- Variable("v", t)
  i <- Variable("i", t)
  System(list(v ~ p$v - n$v, 0 ~ p$i + n$i, i ~ p$i), t, list(v, i), list(),
         systems = list(p, n), name = name)
}

Resistor <- function(name, R = 1) {
  op <- OnePort("oneport")
  u <- toggle_namespacing(op, FALSE)
  Rp <- Parameter("R", default = R)
  extend(System(list(u$v ~ u$i * Rp), t, list(), list(Rp), name = name), op)
}

Capacitor <- function(name, C = 1) {
  op <- OnePort("oneport")
  u <- toggle_namespacing(op, FALSE)
  Cp <- Parameter("C", default = C)
  extend(System(list(D(u$v) ~ u$i / Cp), t, list(), list(Cp), name = name), op)
}

ConstantVoltage <- function(name, V = 1) {
  op <- OnePort("oneport")
  u <- toggle_namespacing(op, FALSE)
  Vp <- Parameter("V", default = V)
  extend(System(list(Vp ~ u$v), t, list(), list(Vp), name = name), op)
}
```

The circuit: the source drives the resistor and the capacitor in series,
and the negative side is grounded.

```{r}
resistor <- Resistor("resistor", R = 2)
capacitor <- Capacitor("capacitor", C = 1)
vsource <- ConstantVoltage("source", V = 1)
ground <- Ground("ground")
rc <- System(
  list(connect(vsource$p, resistor$p),
       connect(resistor$n, capacitor$p),
       connect(capacitor$n, vsource$n),
       connect(capacitor$n, ground$g)),
  t, systems = list(resistor, capacitor, vsource, ground), name = "rc")
hierarchy(rc)
```

Expanding the connections gives 20 equations in 20 unknowns: the element
equations plus, for each connection, equal voltages and a current balance.

```{r}
ex <- expand_connections(rc)
c(equations = length(equations(ex)), unknowns = length(unknowns(ex)))
pp(tail(equations(ex), 7))
```

`mtkcompile()` reduces this to a single differential equation for the
capacitor voltage; the other 19 variables become observed. The compiled
equation refers to the observed current `capacitor₊i`, and
`full_equations()` substitutes the observed equations to give the familiar
form `dv/dt = (V - v) / (R C)`.

```{r}
rc_c <- mtkcompile(rc)
rc_c
pp(full_equations(rc_c))
```

Since `rc_c` is complete, `rc_c$capacitor$v` refers to the capacitor voltage
directly. The capacitor starts discharged; the voltage approaches the source
voltage as `1 - exp(-t / (R * C))`, and the current decays from `V / R`.
`plot(sol)` draws the unknowns against time; the figure below samples the
dense output directly to show an observed variable next to the state.

```{r}
prob <- ODEProblem(rc_c, list(rc_c$capacitor$v ~ 0), c(0, 10))
sol <- solve(prob, Tsit5(), reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-10)
sol$retcode
tt <- c(1, 2, 5, 10)
cbind(t = tt,
      v_capacitor = sol(tt, idxs = rc_c$capacitor$v),
      analytic = 1 - exp(-tt / 2),
      i_resistor = sol(tt, idxs = rc_c$resistor$i))
tg <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 200)
matplot(tg, cbind(sol(tg, idxs = rc_c$capacitor$v), sol(tg, idxs = rc_c$resistor$i)),
        type = "l", lty = 1, col = c("black", "firebrick"), xlab = "t", ylab = "")
legend("right", c("capacitor voltage", "resistor current"), lty = 1,
       col = c("black", "firebrick"), bty = "n")
```

The parameters keep their defaults from the component constructors and can
be overridden in the problem, here halving the resistance:

```{r}
prob2 <- ODEProblem(rc_c, list(rc_c$capacitor$v ~ 0, rc_c$resistor$R ~ 1), c(0, 10))
sol2 <- solve(prob2, Tsit5(), reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-10)
c(simulated = sol2(2, idxs = rc_c$capacitor$v), analytic = 1 - exp(-2))
```
